places.history:
## A tuberculosis hospital in the Småland forests

Målilla Sanatorium was founded in the 1910s at Målilla in Hultsfred Municipality, Småland, as a specialised institution for pulmonary tuberculosis. Patients lived for long periods in isolation-oriented wards designed around rest, air and regimented medical routines. The buildings and landscape still communicate that medical purpose: long corridors, patient rooms, treatment spaces and the quiet weight of an era when TB shaped public health across Sweden.

## Closure, decay and heritage reuse

After tuberculosis treatment declined and the institution eventually closed, buildings entered a second life as an abandoned medical site — then, in parts, as a heritage and museum-oriented destination with guided tours. Preservation and decay sit side by side: peeling paint, empty beds and institutional architecture create the visual language that later made the site famous on television, while heritage stewards work to keep access legal, safe and historically grounded.

## Spökjakt Season 3 premiere

Målilla Sanatorium opened Season 3 of Familjen Lundell's Spökjakt (Episode 1, 2021) with investigators including Joakim and Jonna Lundell alongside LaxTon Ghost Sweden. That premiere cemented national recognition: searchers looking for "Målilla Sanatorium", "Spökjakt sanatorium" or "abandoned hospital Sweden" consistently find this location. Haunted Sweden scores it among the map's LEGENDARY tier for recognition while insisting that TV atmosphere is not the same as proven haunting.

## How Haunted Sweden catalogues the site

We list Målilla under Abandoned Place / medical history, note guided-visit access when offered, and keep family-friendly set to no because of intensity and subject matter. Night access is not recommended without official permission. Source material should always privilege medical history and lawful tours over trespassing narratives.

## Visiting responsibly

Book museum or heritage tours when available. Respect barriers, private property and staff instructions. The site's power comes from real illness and isolation in Swedish history — sensational break-ins undermine both safety and the dignity of that past.

## Architecture of care and control

Sanatorium design in early twentieth-century Sweden favoured light, air and separation. Long wings, verandas and regimented corridors were medical tools as much as buildings. Walking those corridors today — on a lawful tour — is a lesson in how society once managed contagious fear. That educational layer is why Haunted Sweden refuses to treat Målilla as a disposable creepy abandoned hospital meme.

## Media amplification without myth inflation

Spökjakt made Målilla nationally searchable overnight. Search Console impressions follow that fame. Our job is to convert curiosity into informed visits: book the right tour, know the medical backstory, and leave folklore labelled as folklore. We link the official Spökjakt playlist for viewers who want the television context without confusing it for a Haunted Sweden team report.

## Regional context in Småland

Småland's haunted map mixes manors, castles and tragedy sites across large distances. Målilla rewards travellers who accept a dedicated drive rather than a casual detour. Pairing it with Berga Herrgård or a Kalmar day requires realistic timing. Use our nearby and related sections to build an honest itinerary instead of stacking too many stops.
places.legend:
## Atmosphere and folklore

Visitors and guides describe heaviness in corridors, unexplained sounds, and ward-related folklore. These accounts circulate widely online and in TV framing. Haunted Sweden records them as anecdotal atmosphere — not laboratory evidence.

## What Spökjakt showed

The Season 3 premiere used decaying interiors for investigative television: darkness, medical props and emotional stakes. That production value drives tourism curiosity; it does not by itself prove paranormal activity.

## Separating medical tragedy from ghost stories

Tuberculosis wards were places of hope, fear, recovery and death. Responsible dark tourism starts with that medical truth. Ghost narratives may layer on top, but they should never erase the patients and staff who lived the history.

## Nearby haunted places

Within a broader Småland / Southeast Sweden loop, consider Berga Herrgård, Teleborgs Slott, Kalmar Slott and other manor or castle stops on the Haunted Sweden map — plan distances carefully; Målilla is more remote than West Sweden castle clusters.

## Common claim patterns

Online forums recycle the same motifs: footsteps in empty wards, voices near former patient rooms, oppressive air in stairwells. Pattern repetition can mean shared cultural script as easily as shared anomaly. Haunted Sweden logs motifs without crowning a single true ghost narrative.

## Safety and ethics first

Asbestos-era buildings, unstable floors and private security are real risks at many abandoned medical sites worldwide. Even when Målilla offers heritage tours, assume restrictions exist for structural and legal reasons. Never force entry. Never disturb memorial or medical artefacts. Never film patients' descendants' trauma for clicks.

## Future Haunted Sweden investigation goals

Document lawful access routes, capture exterior photography with permission, collect staff-approved historical timelines, and compare TV editing choices with on-the-ground acoustics and lighting. Until that visit happens, this landing page remains the best public brief we can offer searchers landing from Google.

places.historySv:
## Ett tuberkulossjukhus i Smålandsskogarna

Målilla sanatorium grundades på 1910-talet i Målilla, Hultsfreds kommun i Småland, som en specialiserad institution för lungtuberkulos. Patienter vistades under långa perioder i isoleringsinriktade salar byggda kring vila, luft och strikta medicinska rutiner. Byggnader och landskap förmedlar fortfarande det medicinska syftet: långa korridorer, patientrum, behandlingsytor och den tysta tyngden från en tid då TBC formade folkhälsan i Sverige.

## Nedläggning, förfall och kulturarv

När tuberkulosvården minskade och institutionen så småningom stängde fick byggnaderna ett andra liv som övergiven medicinsk plats — och delvis som kulturarvs- och museiinriktad destination med guidningar. Bevarande och förfall står sida vid sida: flagnande färg, tomma sängar och institutionsarkitektur skapar det visuella språk som senare gjorde platsen känd på TV, medan kulturarvsförvaltare arbetar för laglig, säker och historiskt förankrad tillgång.

## Spökjakt säsong 3-premiär

Målilla sanatorium öppnade säsong 3 av Familjen Lundells Spökjakt (avsnitt 1, 2021) med bland andra Joakim och Jonna Lundell samt LaxTon Ghost Sweden. Premiären cementerade nationell igenkänning: den som söker "Målilla Sanatorium", "Spökjakt sanatorium" eller "övergivet sjukhus Sverige" hittar ofta hit. Haunted Sweden placerar platsen i LEGENDARY-skiktet för igenkänning men understryker att TV-atmosfär inte är detsamma som bevisad hemsökelse.

## Hur Haunted Sweden katalogiserar platsen

Vi listar Målilla under Abandoned Place / medicinhistoria, noterar guidat besök när det erbjuds, och sätter familjevänligt till nej på grund av intensitet och ämne. Nattbesök rekommenderas inte utan officiellt tillstånd. Källmaterial ska alltid prioritera medicinhistoria och lagliga turer framför intrångsberättelser.

## Besök ansvarsfullt

Boka museum- eller kulturarvsturer när de finns. Respektera avspärrningar, privat mark och personalens instruktioner. Platsens kraft kommer från verklig sjukdom och isolering i svensk historia — sensationalistiska inbrott undergräver både säkerhet och värdighet.

## Vårdens och kontrollens arkitektur

Sanatoriedesign i tidigt 1900-talets Sverige gynnade ljus, luft och separation. Långa flyglar, verandor och regisserade korridorer var medicinska verktyg lika mycket som byggnader. Att gå de korridorerna i dag — på en laglig tur — är en lektion i hur samhället en gång hanterade smittsam rädsla. Det utbildande lagret är varför Haunted Sweden vägrar behandla Målilla som ett slit-och-släng-meme om övergivna sjukhus.

## Medieförstärkning utan mytinflation

Spökjakt gjorde Målilla nationellt sökbart över en natt. Search Console-exponering följer det ryktet. Vår uppgift är att omvandla nyfikenhet till informerade besök: boka rätt tur, känna den medicinska bakgrunden och låta folklore vara märkt som folklore. Vi länkar den officiella Spökjakt-spellistan för den som vill ha TV-kontext utan att blanda ihop den med en Haunted Sweden-teamrapport.

## Regional kontext i Småland

Smålands hemsökta karta blandar herrgårdar, slott och tragediplatser över stora avstånd. Målilla belönar resenärer som accepterar en dedikerad bilresa snarare än en tillfällig avstickare. Att para med Berga Herrgård eller en Kalmar-dag kräver realistisk timing. Använd våra närliggande- och relaterat-sektioner för en ärlig itinerary i stället för för många stopp.
places.legendSv:
## Atmosfär och folklore

Besökare och guider beskriver tyngd i korridorer, oförklarliga ljud och salrelaterad folklore. Berättelserna cirkulerar brett online och i TV-ramar. Haunted Sweden registrerar dem som anekdotisk atmosfär — inte laboratoriebevis.

## Vad Spökjakt visade

Säsong 3-premiären använde förfallna interiörer för utrednings-TV: mörker, medicinska rekvisita och emotionella insatser. Den produktionskvaliteten driver turistnyfikenhet; den bevisar inte i sig paranormal aktivitet.

## Separera medicinsk tragedi från spökhistorier

Tuberkulossalar var platser för hopp, rädsla, tillfrisknande och död. Ansvarsfull dark tourism börjar i den medicinska sanningen. Spökberättelser kan läggas ovanpå, men de får aldrig sudda ut patienter och personal som levde historien.

## Närliggande hemsökta platser

I en bredare Småland-/sydöstsverigeslinga kan du överväga Berga Herrgård, Teleborgs Slott, Kalmar Slott och andra herrgårds- eller slottsstopp på Haunted Swedens karta — planera avstånd noga; Målilla ligger mer avsides än Västsveriges slottskluster.

## Vanliga påståendemönster

Forum online återanvänder samma motiv: fotsteg i tomma salar, röster nära tidigare patientrum, tryckande luft i trapphus. Upprepning kan betyda delad kulturell manusmall lika gärna som delad anomali. Haunted Sweden loggar motiv utan att kröna en enda sann spökberättelse.

## Säkerhet och etik först

Byggnader från asbesttid, ostabila golv och privat bevakning är verkliga risker på många övergivna medicinska platser. Även när Målilla erbjuder kulturarvsturer, utgå från att restriktioner finns av strukturella och juridiska skäl. Tvinga aldrig intrång. Stör aldrig minnes- eller medicinska föremål. Filma aldrig ättlingars trauma för klick.

## Framtida mål för Haunted Sweden-utredning

Dokumentera lagliga tillträdesvägar, ta exteriörfoto med tillstånd, samla personalgodkända historiska tidslinjer och jämför TV-klippval med akustik och ljus på plats. Tills det besöket sker är denna landningssida den bästa publika briefen vi kan ge sökare från Google.

places.name: Vadstena Klosterhotell
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Vadstena Klosterhotell is one of Sweden's most historically significant overnight stays — a working hotel woven through the remains of Vadstena Abbey, motherhouse of the Bridgettine Order founded by Saint Birgitta in the 1300s. For more than six centuries the site has shifted from double monastery to soldiers' home, hospital, prison, asylum and finally guest rooms among medieval stone, cloisters and chapter houses beside Lake Vättern. Guests and local tradition describe footsteps in empty corridors, whispers, and the sense of being watched after dark. Haunted Sweden lists it as a top Östergötland candidate for future overnight investigation (EVP, night photography, staff interviews) — folklore and reports are presented separately from documented history. Book through the hotel; respect guest privacy and house rules.

places.history: DOCUMENTED: Vadstena Abbey (Vadstena kloster) was founded as the motherhouse of the Bridgettine Order after Saint Birgitta (Birgitta Birgersdotter) received her revelations; monastic life on the site dates to the 1300s. The community functioned as a double monastery with both monks and nuns under the Bridgettine rule until the Reformation. After 1527 the monastery was gradually dissolved, though religious and institutional use of the complex continued in new forms. Documented later roles for parts of the ensemble include Krigsmanshus (housing for injured soldiers), general hospital, correctional institution, prison facilities and mental-health care — centuries of illness, confinement and death layered onto monastic isolation. Several original medieval structures remain integrated into the modern Vadstena Klosterhotell at Lasarettsgatan 3, including some of Sweden's oldest preserved non-religious buildings within a living hotel environment. The abbey church and pilgrimage heritage remain central to Vadstena's identity; the hotel markets stays in monk cells, chapter-house settings and courtyard wings. Sources: parish and regional history, Bridgettine order scholarship, building conservation records, hotel heritage descriptions.

places.name: Hörle Herrgård
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Near the Lagan River outside Värnamo, Hörle Herrgård is one of Småland's finest late Carolingian manor houses — completed in 1746 on the fortunes of Hörle Bruk, the ironworks founded in 1659. Architect Bengt Wilhelm Carlberg and interior influences from Carl Hårleman and court painter Johan Pasch shaped an estate that still feels like stepping into the 1700s after extensive 2010s restoration. Local folklore is dominated by the White Lady: Anna Margareta Lilliecreutz, who built the manor through three marriages, is said to walk the halls in white before vanishing without a trace. Visitors and tradition describe sightings, footsteps, creaking doors and an unseen presence on upper floors — Haunted Sweden presents these as legend and witness stories, not verified hauntings. A protected historic building (byggnadsminne, 1992) with exceptional visual identity and very high premium investigation potential.

places.history: DOCUMENTED: Hörle Bruk was founded in 1659 by Dutch entrepreneur Justus Baak during Sweden's iron-industry expansion along the Lagan valley outside Värnamo. The manor (Hörle Herrgård) was developed from the early 1700s through the efforts of Anna Margareta Lilliecreutz and her three husbands, and was completed in 1746. The building is attributed to architect Bengt Wilhelm Carlberg, with interior work influenced by Carl Hårleman and decorative painting associated with royal court painter Johan Pasch. The estate reflects generations of iron wealth, family disputes, inheritance struggles and noble residence — residents living and dying within the walls across centuries. Hörle Herrgård was declared a protected historic building (byggnadsminne) in 1992 and underwent extensive restoration in the 2010s while preserving much of its original character. Today it ranks among Småland's most impressive and best-preserved manor houses, set among forest and waterways near the former bruk landscape.
places.legend: THE WHITE LADY (folklore — not historically verified as paranormal): The estate's defining story names Anna Margareta Lilliecreutz as the spirit who remains at Hörle — a white female figure reported moving through rooms and corridors before suddenly disappearing. The legend has been retold for generations and is among Småland's best-known manor ghost traditions, layered onto the documented life of the woman who shaped the house. FOLKLORE & WITNESS REPORTS: Sightings of a white figure, feelings of being watched, footsteps in empty rooms, unexplained creaking, doors opening or closing, unseen presence on upper floors, and strange sensations near windows — presented as local legend and subjective reports, not verified paranormal events. NOTABLE AREAS: (1) Main manor hall — heart of White Lady sightings. (2) Upper floors — footsteps and sounds. (3) Historic staircases — strong atmospheric value. (4) Manor grounds — forest, river setting, folklore after sunset. ATMOSPHERE: Elegant 1746 interiors, grand staircase, candlelit mood, isolation in fog and winter darkness, blue hour contrast between beauty and mystery. FUTURE HAUNTED SWEDEN MISSION: exterior and night photography, archive research, EVP in main hall, historian and witness interviews, fog exploration — premium content potential VERY HIGH. BEST CONDITIONS: autumn evenings, heavy fog, rain, winter darkness, blue hour.

places.name: Toftaholm Herrgård
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Beside Lake Vidöstern in Småland, Toftaholm Herrgård is one of Sweden's most famous haunted manor hotels — documented estate history from 1389, ties to the Stenbock family, and folklore that the hotel itself shares with guests. Gustav Vasa is said to have visited through Stenbock connections; today's main house dates from 1871 after fire destroyed earlier buildings, while Den Gyllene Abborren inn has stood since 1640. The defining legend is Mats, a servant who loved the count's daughter, vanished during her wedding, and was found dead in a guest room — his grave near Mats-stenen and stories of Room 324 keep the tale alive. Reports include footsteps, cold spots, doors opening, and a gentle male presence; the manor describes Mats as a friendly spirit. Haunted Sweden lists premium overnight investigation potential (Room 324, EVP, Mats-stenen) — book officially and respect guest privacy.

places.history: DOCUMENTED: Toftaholm's recorded history begins in 1389 when the estate was held by Jöns Skötta, later ennobled as Stenbock. A fortified manor was built on nearby Stenhusholmen in the 1400s; for centuries the property remained tied to the influential Stenbock family. Tradition holds that Gustav Vasa visited the estate and met his future wife Katarina Stenbock through this family network. The main residence was rebuilt after a devastating fire in the 1800s; the present manor house dates from 1871. Den Gyllene Abborren (The Golden Perch), the historic inn on the estate, traces to 1640 and is among the oldest preserved structures on the property. Today Toftaholm operates as a manor hotel beside Vidöstern, popular with history visitors and paranormal enthusiasts alike.

When the count arranged her marriage to another nobleman, Mats disappeared during the wedding festivities. He was later found dead, having taken his own life in a manor guest room. His grave is said to lie near Mats-stenen on the estate. Folklore holds that Mats never left Toftaholm. (2) Main manor — historic corridors and guest rooms. (3) Mats-stenen — grave site in the legend. (4) Den Gyllene Abborren — inn since 1640. ATMOSPHERE: Forest, lake, candlelit dining, quiet nights. places.name: Åmåls Stadshotell
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Åmåls Stadshotell stands at Kungsgatan 9 in the heart of Åmål — one of the town's most recognizable buildings and a classic Swedish city-hotel mystery. The present hotel rose in 1903–1904 after the great fire of 15 January 1902 destroyed its predecessor; architect Ture Stenberg's façade still anchors the old town between Kungsgatan, Södra Ågatan and Norra Långgatan, with preserved staircases, ballroom and dining rooms from a century of travellers, celebrations and quiet tragedies. Documented history layers three fires on this plot (1645, 1809, 1902), an acetylene explosion that delayed the 1905 opening, and byggnadsminne protection since 1978. Swedish media have reported guest and staff anecdotes — moving door handles, cutlery falling, footsteps and a sense of being watched — presented here as folklore and witness accounts, not proven hauntings. Haunted Sweden rates it strong for atmosphere and overnight investigation (historic corridors, rainy evenings, weekday silence) with medium research confidence and medium–high premium potential pending a future verification mission.

places.history: DOCUMENTED: Åmåls Stadshotell at Kungsgatan 9 (kvarteret Liljan Mindre) occupies one of Åmål's most central plots. Municipal and heritage sources record that buildings on the site burned three times: after Norwegian troops ravaged the young town in 1645; in April 1809 when commerce advisor Bengt Norström's house was lost; and on 15 January 1902 when the previous city hotel and Hammargården were destroyed in a major fire that damaged much of the old town. The current hotel was designed by architect A. Ture Stenberg and built 1903–1904; opening was delayed when an acetylene lighting plant exploded on 29 November 1904, and the hotel finally opened in April 1905. It became a listed historic building (byggnadsminne) on 17 April 1978. Later changes include 1940s–1950s exterior simplification, a 1960s north extension, municipal ownership and renovation from 1999, and operation today with roughly thirty rooms plus preserved stairwells, ballroom and dining halls. Sources: Åmål municipality heritage pages, Bebyggelseregistret (RAÄ), Swedish Wikipedia, hotel heritage materials.

Haunted Sweden presents these as subjective accounts and urban hotel folklore, not proven paranormal activity. No single historical death on the property is verified here as a named haunting cause; emotional residue from generations of guests, fires and rebuilds is interpretive. places.name: Överås Slott
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Överås Slott at Danska Vägen 20 is one of Gothenburg's most iconic castle-like mansions — a white Italian Renaissance palace built in the 1860s for James J. Dickson, son of the Scottish merchant dynasty that helped shape the city. Lavish Dickson-era parties, a Methodist seminary from 1924, and preserved interiors (stucco halls, the self-supporting staircase, Nordiska Kompaniet billiard room) sit above Örgryte with English parkland and ancient trees. The site's legend is the Woman in Black (Svarta damen): folklore and witness reports from 1924 onward describe a black-clad figure, creaking stairs, and corridors where she vanishes — often linked in local tradition to a tragic nineteenth-century story of a young woman at the estate. Göteborg media and haunted-place guides treat Överås as the city's signature manor ghost story. Haunted Sweden presents all paranormal accounts as folklore, not proven fact — with very high premium potential for exterior night work, archive research, and future verification.

places.history: DOCUMENTED: Överås at Danska Vägen 20 in Göteborg (Örgryte/Bö) is a palatial manor built in the first half of the 1860s — sources cite completion around 1861–1865 — for James J. Dickson (James Dickson d.y.), of the Scottish-origin Dickson merchant family central to Gothenburg's industrial and philanthropic history. Architect V. Bulnois won James Dickson's competition; builder A. Krüger executed an English-influenced Italian Renaissance villa described by heritage staff as a 'pearl' among the city's merchant palaces. Earlier structures on the plot included a 1770s timber house; the estate name and lands have deeper roots (local history notes settlement and conflict in the Älvsborg region from the 1500s onward). The Dicksons hosted grand society events; Robert Dickson later subdivided land for Örgryte trädgårdsstad (1906). The city acquired the property around 1907 but could not use it for civic receptions because the will forbade alcohol on site. From 1923 the building served the Methodist Church's theological seminary (courses began 16 February 1924); pastoral training continued for decades. Later uses include Gothia Academy offices, event hire via Överås Slott AB (weddings and functions), and planned care-housing extensions (Wallenstam purchase, 2017). Preserved interiors include stucco walls, the great self-supporting stair, library and billiard room with Nordiska Kompaniet fittings. Sources: overasslott.se, Swedish Wikipedia, Göteborgs historia, Riksantikvarieämbetet descriptions.
places.legend: THE WOMAN IN BLACK / SVARTA DAMEN (folklore — not verified as paranormal): Gothenburg's best-known manor ghost legend. Witness tradition dates to 1924 when the building became a seminary — stories include a Finnish theology student who allegedly fled after a black-clothed, veiled woman entered through tall windows, and other students seeing a translucent older woman in a high-necked black dress on a bed edge before she faded toward the ceiling. Reports over generations mention creaking footsteps on main staircases, sounds from upper floors and attics, a silent black female figure in corridors, sudden atmosphere changes, and feelings of being watched. LOCAL FOLKLORE (tragic backstory — partly tied to documented legal narrative in regional press): a young woman staying with the Dickson household in the 1800s lost an infant; after accusations and a trial in which she was acquitted, tradition holds she died by suicide in the attic — linked by researchers such as Sten Ekstrand to the ghost story, though the paranormal connection remains interpretive. NOTABLE AREAS: (1) Main staircases — footsteps. (2) Upper floors — Woman in Black sightings. (3) Historic corridors — core witness zone. (4) English park and old trees — folklore atmosphere after dark. SCORING (editorial): Visual 9.5/10, Historical 9.5/10, Folklore 9/10, Paranormal reputation 8.5/10, Night investigation 8.5/10. FUTURE HAUNTED SWEDEN MISSION: exterior night photography, archive research, EVP only where legally permitted, park exploration, decade comparison of reports — premium potential VERY HIGH. BEST CONDITIONS: autumn fog, rain, winter darkness, blue hour.

places.name: Nyckelhålshuset
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Nyckelhålshuset at Sveagatan 2 in Linnéstaden is one of Gothenburg's quirkiest urban ghost legends — not a castle or ruin, but a 1903 Jugend apartment house famous for its keyhole-shaped entrance and a facade plaque that tells the story itself. The sign claims a tall, headless man haunts the building: "astronomer Arthur Lowell," said to have stayed here during a June 1909 visit while studying Mars and its canals. Haunted Sweden notes that Arthur is almost certainly folklore's twist on the real American astronomer Percival Lowell — and that no strong evidence confirms either the haunting or the stay. What is documented is the architecture, the nickname Nyckelhålshuset, and decades of city guides (Göteborg.com, Atlas Obscura, ghost walks) treating the plaque as part of the building's identity. Visit respectfully from the pavement: rain, fog and late-night Linné streets turn this into pure urban mystery — folklore presented separately from verified history.
places.whyItFitsHauntedSweden: Signature Gothenburg street-level folklore with unique visual identity (keyhole portal + ghost plaque), easy public access for photography and ghost-walk routes, high folklore and urban-mystery scores (9/10 and 10/10), strong contrast to manor-and-castle entries, and high premium potential for night documentation and legend-vs-reality content — research confidence MEDIUM–HIGH; ideal Haunted Gothenburg stop alongside Överås and other city legends.
places.shortDescription: Göteborg's Keyhole House (1903 Jugend) — famous entrance plaque tells of a headless "Arthur Lowell" ghost; urban legend, not verified history.
places.history: DOCUMENTED: Nyckelhålshuset is a residential building at Sveagatan 2 (corner with Risåsgatan) in Linnéstaden, Göteborg, near Skansberget. Built in 1903, it belongs to the era when the Linné district and western Gothenburg expanded with stone apartment houses in Jugend / Art Nouveau style. The nickname Nyckelhålshuset comes from the distinctive keyhole-shaped main entrance — one of the area's most recognizable façades. The property operates as a housing cooperative (Brf Nyckelhålet) with period interiors (high ceilings, mouldings, cast iron) typical of early-1900s Göteborg. Linnéstaden's café culture, parks and tram lines frame a dense historic neighbourhood rather than a rural estate. Sources: Göteborg.com haunted guides, Atlas Obscura, local real-estate heritage descriptions citing byggår 1903.
places.legend: THE HEADLESS MAN & GHOST PLAQUE (folklore — not verified as paranormal): A sign beside the keyhole entrance states (in essence) that the house is haunted by a tall, slim, headless man — identified on the plaque as astronomer "Arthur Lowell," discoverer of Mars canals, who allegedly stayed in a second-floor apartment during a Gothenburg visit 3–16 June 1909. The story is unusual because the legend is displayed on the building itself, not only passed orally. FOLKLORE ANALYSIS: "Arthur Lowell" is widely understood as a playful or mistaken name for Percival Lowell (1855–1916), the real Mars-canal astronomer; his documented link to this specific flat is weak, and the plaque may be artistic or humorous rather than historical. REPORTED URBAN MYTHS (subjective): sightings of a tall headless figure, unease near the entrance, and reputation amplified by ghost walks and media — Haunted Sweden does not treat these as proven hauntings. NOTABLE AREAS: (1) Keyhole entrance + plaque. (2) Entrance hall (stories). (3) Night exterior on Sveagatan. (4) Surrounding Linné streets. SCORING (editorial): Visual 8.5/10, Historical 8/10, Folklore 9/10, Paranormal reputation 8/10, Urban mystery 10/10. FUTURE MISSION: photograph plaque, archive Lowell dates, resident interviews, folklore documentation — premium HIGH. BEST CONDITIONS: rain, fog, winter dark, blue hour, late quiet hours.

Troligen lek med namnet Percival Lowell; ingen stark historisk koppling eller bevisad paranormal aktivitet. OMRÅDEN: nyckelhålsporten, entréhall, fasad nattetid, Linnégator. Urban mystik.

Arthur Lowell på skylten är folklore, sannolikt avsedd som Percival Lowell; huset är lätt att besöka från trottoaren och perfekt på en hemsökt Göteborg-rutt.

places.name: Hôtel Eggers
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Hôtel Eggers at Drottningtorget 2–4 is one of Sweden's oldest continuously operating hotels — founded in 1859 as Jernvägshotellet beside the new Central Station, rebuilt into a Belle Époque palace under Emil and Axel Eggers, and still welcoming guests through wars, emigrations and a century of city life. Documented history meets ghost folklore in the story of Ebba Eggers: after manager Axel Eggers died in 1942, his wife Ebba ran the hotel until she was killed in a plane crash in Denmark on 12 February 1948 — ending the family's era. Local tradition describes a benevolent female presence still watching over the house; guest and staff stories for decades centre on Room 397, footsteps in corridors, and the hush after midnight behind red velvet and chandeliers. Gothenburg haunted guides and Swedish paranormal media (including teams such as LaxTon Ghost Sweden in regional coverage) list Eggers among the city's strongest hotel legends. Haunted Sweden presents all paranormal reports as folklore — with extremely high overnight and premium investigation potential when booked officially.
places.whyItFitsHauntedSweden: Flagship central Gothenburg haunted accommodation: continuous operation since 1859, documented Eggers dynasty and Ebba's 1948 tragedy, Room 397 folklore, press and ghost-walk ubiquity, bookable overnight stays steps from Central Station, Belle Époque visuals (9/10), and extremely high premium content — research confidence HIGH; ideal Haunted Sweden verification target and LaxTon-comparison revisit for Room 397.
places.shortDescription: Sweden's railway-era grand hotel since 1859 at Drottningtorget — Belle Époque luxury, the ghost of Ebba Eggers, and folklore around Room 397.
places.history: DOCUMENTED: Hôtel Eggers occupies a listed corner at Drottningtorget 2–4, ~78 steps from Göteborg Central Station. In 1859, the year after the station opened, traktörskan Wilhelmina Schmidt established Jernvägshotellet for rail travellers — among Sweden's earliest purpose-built traveller lodging. L.E. Lindblad later ran it as Hotel Christiania; Emil Eggers joined as night porter, married into the family, and bought the business in 1883, expanding to a three-storey hotel reopened 5 November 1894 with electric light, private bathrooms and in-room telephones. Son Axel Eggers managed from 1910 until his death in 1942; his wife Ebba Eggers (née spritkassörska at the hotel) took over until 12 February 1948 when she died in an aviation accident in Denmark with multiple fatalities. Göteborg stad had acquired the property in 1944; afterward advocates Hilding and Hans Brodén, then the Ramén family, and later owners continued operations. The hotel cites guests from royalty and artists to diplomats and spies during both world wars; parts of the building date to 1820 with older city-wall remnants below. Today ~69 individually styled rooms, conference spaces, restaurant and bar preserve sekelskiftes character. Sources: hoteleggers.se history pages, folk o folk, hotel filmography list.
places.legend: EBBA EGGERS (folklore — not verified as paranormal): Gothenburg's signature hotel ghost. After Axel Eggers' death (1942), Ebba ran Hôtel Eggers until her fatal 1948 crash; local stories say she never truly left — a kindly female presence checking that 'everything is managed correctly' (hotel and media tone). ROOM 397: The room number most associated with Ebba sightings in haunted-city guides and guest lore; also used as a film location (e.g. Fyra år till) — the hotel does not officially market a 'haunted room,' but folklore consistently links 397 to the legend. WITNESS REPORTS & MEDIA (unverified): woman seen in or near 397, cleaning staff and guests describing figures, feeling watched alone at night, corridor footsteps, cold spots, doors and sounds — repeated across decades in Göteborg ghost lists. PARANORMAL CREATORS: Swedish teams including LaxTon Ghost Sweden are commonly cited in regional haunted-hotel discussions; Haunted Sweden treats prior videos as media folklore, not scientific proof. NOTABLE AREAS: Room 397, historic corridors, staircases, lobby/reception. SCORING (editorial): Visual 9/10, Historical 10/10, Folklore 9.5/10, Paranormal reputation 9/10, Overnight 10/10. FUTURE MISSION: licensed overnight in 397, EVP, night photography, staff interviews, archive research, LaxTon comparison — premium EXTREMELY HIGH. BEST CONDITIONS: overnight stay, rain, winter dark, quiet weekdays, after midnight in corridors (with permission).
places.safetyNote: Active hotel — book only through official channels. Respect guests, staff, fire rules and night quiet. Do not film or investigate in corridors or other guests' rooms without permission; room requests (including 397) depend on availability.

places.name: Gathenhielmska Huset
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Gathenhielmska Huset at Stigbergstorget 7 is one of Gothenburg's most authentic 1700s survivors — a grey timber merchant palace built circa 1743–1747 in Majorna, named for privateer Lars Gathenhielm ("Lasse i Gatan") though he died in 1718 before the house rose. Konvojkommissarie Johan Hansson Busck, married to Lars's sister Anna Thalena Gathe, erected the Carolingian/late Baroque home within the Gathenhielm cultural reserve; it became Sweden's first building protected under the 1942 heritage act (10 July 1943) and remains one of the city's five oldest secular structures. Gothenburg folklore says Lars still rides from his grave in Onsala church on dark autumn nights — neighbours report clattering hooves toward the façade and, in some tales, a fiery horse and rider. Haunted Sweden separates documented maritime history from legend: interior tours and candlelit events reveal preserved salons, while mist and rain on Stigbergstorget amplify the phantom-rider story — very high premium potential for a Haunted Gothenburg route.
places.whyItFitsHauntedSweden: Top-tier Gothenburg folklore site with nationally documented heritage (first protected building in the city), direct link to Great Northern War privateering, preserved 1740s timber architecture, public square access, phantom-horse legend in press and guides, strong night-exterior atmosphere, and very high storytelling and verification potential — research confidence HIGH; complements Hotel Eggers, Överås and Nyckelhålshuset on a central-west haunted circuit.
places.shortDescription: Gothenburg's 1740s timber manor at Stigbergstorget — first heritage-protected building in the city, tied to kapare Lars Gathenhielm and phantom horse-hoof folklore.
places.history: DOCUMENTED: Gathenhielmska Huset stands at Stigbergstorget 7 in Majorna (kvarter Gatenhjelm), within the Gathenhielm cultural reserve opposite today's maritime museum quarter. Lars Gathenhielm (1689–1718), Charles XII's famed privateer "Lasse i Gatan," received land at Gamla Varvet / Stigberget in 1717 for his corsair service; he died 25 April 1718 (aged 28) and is buried with his wife Ingela Hammar in Onsala church — he never lived in this house. His sister Anna Thalena Gathe and brother-in-law Johan Hansson Busck (1690–1756) bought the plot (deed 1737) and built the present structure circa 1743–1747: Göteborg's only preserved large wooden merchant residence from the mid-1700s, among the five oldest secular buildings in the city, with hipped roof and grey timber cladding imitating stone. On 10 July 1943 it became the first building in Göteborg protected under the 1942 law on culturally significant buildings; protection was clarified in 1964 to cover exterior, interior and plot. Owners included the Busck heirs, Tranchell, von Aken, and 140 years of the Dahlström/Tham families until Göteborg municipality purchased in 1986; Higab manages today with association use, preserved rooms (Kungsrummet, Versaillessalongen, Stora salongen) and garden. Sources: Wikipedia, Higab, kulturreservatet.se, Sjöfartsmuseet, Expressen GT.
places.legend: LASSE I GATAN / PHANTOM RIDER (folklore — not verified as paranormal): Despite posthumous construction, popular belief binds the house to Lars Gathenhielm. On dark autumn evenings passers-by in Majorna have long reported clattering horse hooves approaching Stigbergstorget — interpreted as Lars rising from his Onsala grave to visit the site linked to his name and family. Some stories add a headless or fiery horse, sparks from hooves, and a rider hurrying to a waiting wife — mixing saga with the real Ingela legend. INTERIOR FOLKLORE: visitors and guides describe heavy atmosphere, sense of being watched, and emotional weight in candlelit 1700s rooms — subjective, not scientifically verified. NOTABLE AREAS: (1) Front entrance / square — hoofbeats legend. (2) Historic ground-floor and upper salons. (3) Staircases. (4) Gathenhielmska garden. SCORING (editorial): Visual 9/10, Historical 10/10, Folklore 9/10, Paranormal reputation 8/10, Night investigation 8.5/10. FUTURE HAUNTED SWEDEN MISSION: night exterior audio, archive research, guided-tour documentation, EVP only with permission, folklore vs history film — premium VERY HIGH. BEST CONDITIONS: autumn fog, rain, winter dark, blue hour. NOTE: Karl XII never visited the house despite "Kungsrummet" symbolism.
places.safetyNote: Heritage house and event venue — view the exterior freely from Stigbergstorget; enter only during official openings, tours or booked events. Do not trespass on the plot after hours, disturb residents nearby, or block the square.
places.shortDescriptionSv: Göteborgs 1740-tals träborgarhus vid Stigbergstorget — stadens första byggnadsminne, kopplat till kaparen Lars Gathenhielm och folklore om fantomhovar.
places.historySv: DOKUMENTERAT: Gathenhielmska huset 1743–1747 av Johan Busck, svåger till Lars Gathenhielm (död 1718). Ett av fem äldsta profana husen i Göteborg; första skyddade byggnaden 10 juli 1943. Ingår i Gathenhielms kulturreservat i Majorna; Higab förvaltar, bevarade salar och trädgård.
places.legendSv: LASSE I GATAN (folklore): Klapprande hovar mot huset höstnätter — kaparen ska resa från graven i Onsala. Ibland eldsprutande häst och ryttare. Ej verifierat paranormalt. OMRÅDEN: entré, Stigbergstorget, interiör vid guidning, trädgård.
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummarySv: Gathenhielmska huset vid Stigbergstorget — 1740-talets träpalats och Göteborgs första byggnadsminne, namngivet efter kaparen Lars Gathenhielm trots att huset uppfördes efter hans död. Folklore om fantomhovar och den rastlöse ryttaren gör platsen till en av stadens starkaste maritima spöklegender — historia och saga tydligt åtskilda.
places.safetyNoteSv: Byggnadsminnesmärkt hus och eventlokal – betrakta fasaden fritt från Stigbergstorget; gå endast in vid officiella öppningar, visningar eller bokade evenemang. Trespassera inte på tomten efter stängning eller stör grannar.

places.name: Gripsholms Värdshus
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Gripsholms Värdshus in Mariefred is among Sweden's oldest continuously operating inns — granted privileges on 13 February 1609 by order of King Charles IX so the town's burghers would no longer house the court at their own expense. For more than four centuries it has stood beside Gripsholm Castle on ground once belonging to the Carthusian monastery Pax Mariae, welcoming royalty, merchants, officers and travellers through war, plague eras and changing ownership. Documented hospitality history meets local folklore: guests and staff describe footsteps in empty corridors, unexplained voices, doors that open or close on their own, cold spots, and sightings often linked to monastic figures — rooms 115 and 210 and the wine cellar appear most often in reports. Haunted Sweden separates royal and civic records from witness accounts and legend. Book officially; autumn and winter nights, with a walk toward the castle after dark, make the inn an exceptional overnight investigation setting.
places.whyItFitsHauntedSweden: Flagship Södermanland haunted accommodation: inn privileges since 1609, direct royal connection to Charles IX and Gripsholm Castle, monastery-ground heritage (Pax Mariae), more than 400 years of documented hospitality, walking distance between inn and castle for paired night investigations, traditional interiors with high visual rating (9.5/10), historical value 10/10, folklore and paranormal reputation 8.5/10, overnight investigation potential 10/10 — Haunted Sweden Score 9.4. Premium content potential VERY HIGH; research confidence HIGH. Ideal Mariefred route stop and future verification mission (overnight, EVP in corridors, staff interviews, archive research, castle night walk).
places.shortDescription: Sweden's royal-era inn since 1609 beside Gripsholm Castle — four centuries of hospitality, monastic ground, and enduring ghost folklore in Mariefred.
places.history: DOCUMENTED: Gripsholms Värdshus at Kyrkogatan 1, Mariefred (Södermanland), beside Gripsholm Castle on Lake Mälaren. In the early 1600s Mariefred had no dedicated coaching inn; burghers were obliged to lodge travellers, and court servants of Charles IX — who frequently resided at Gripsholm — were housed without payment as a form of tax. Burgher protests in 1609 led to a royal letter of privilege dated 13 February 1609 naming the first innkeeper, Jocim (Joachim) Smock from Germany, previously a Stockholm tavern keeper; the Smock Room still commemorates him. The site lies on land of the former Carthusian monastery Pax Mariae (Mary's Peace), dissolved mid-1520s, which gave Mariefred its name; during 1980s renovations monastic remains were found and some are preserved in the wine cellar. Castle accounts mention a gästgivare building as early as 1592, but the exact first inn location is uncertain; the present plot (gård 7–8, kvarteret Källaren) was built by at least 1613. The business later operated under names including Stadshotellet and Stadskällaren. The current main building dates largely to the mid-18th century; after a 1957 lightning fire at a Lottenlund site that briefly carried the Gripsholms värdshus name, the Mariefred inn was extensively restored and reopened in 1989 with a 12-metre extension housing royal suites and parquet floors modelled on Swedish castle originals. Across four centuries the inn has hosted royalty, noble families, merchants, military officers and travellers, surviving wars, epidemics and ownership changes while remaining one of Sweden's oldest operating inns. Nearby Gripsholm Castle (Gustav Vasa foundation; Charles IX renovation; later royal residence, prison and State Portrait Collection) shares the same royal-civic landscape. DARK HISTORY (documented context, not paranormal claims): centuries of arrivals and departures imply ordinary deaths from age, illness and accident among guests and staff; Mariefred and Södermanland endured plague periods, wartime hardship and castle dramas that form the emotional backdrop of the place — Haunted Sweden does not invent specific hauntings from these facts alone.
places.legend: FOLKLORE & WITNESS REPORTS (not scientifically verified): Guests and staff for many decades describe footsteps in empty corridors, unexplained voices, doors opening or closing by themselves, cold spots, a sense of being watched, and occasional sightings of figures in grey-brown monastic habits with dark hoods — commonly linked in local tradition to Carthusian monks of Pax Mariae rather than to named historical individuals. Rooms 115 and 210 are most frequently cited; some guests report waking to a duvet moving as if tucked in, described as a gentle rather than hostile presence. The wine cellar is repeatedly named in staff stories (shadows, odd sounds, atmosphere). Media and paranormal sites (e.g. Myling and Swedish ghost lists) also weave castle lore into the Mariefred picture — including older anecdotes of moving door handles in castle wings — but Haunted Sweden treats castle reports as related regional folklore, not proof of activity at the inn. SPECIAL AREAS: historic guest rooms (original detailing + unexplained-experience reports); old corridors (footsteps, heavy atmosphere after midnight); restaurant and dining rooms (centuries as a gathering place); courtyard with views toward Gripsholm Castle. ATMOSPHERE: traditional Swedish inn, wooden interiors, antiques, candlelit dining, quiet post-midnight corridors, charming Mariefred streets — strongest in autumn, winter darkness and rain. INVESTIGATION IDEAS: overnight stay; EVP in historic corridors; night photography; staff interviews; compare guest reports; night walk between inn and castle; contrast inn legends with castle legends. BEST CONDITIONS: overnight, autumn evenings, winter dark, rain, quiet weekdays. Separate DOCUMENTED history (privileges 1609, Smock, monastery ground, building phases) from WITNESS REPORTS and FOLKLORE above.
places.safetyNote: Active historic hotel and restaurant — book only through official channels (gripsholms-vardshus.se). Respect guests, staff, fire rules and night quiet. Do not film or investigate in corridors, the wine cellar or other guests' rooms without permission; room requests (including 115 or 210) depend on availability. When walking to Gripsholm Castle after dark, stay on public paths and follow castle opening and safety rules.
places.shortDescriptionSv: Sveriges kungliga värdshus sedan 1609 vid Gripsholms slott — fyra århundraden av gästfrihet, klostergrund och bestående spökfolklore i Mariefred.
places.historySv: DOKUMENTERAT: Gripsholms värdshus, Kyrkogatan 1 i Mariefred (Södermanland), intill Gripsholms slott. Tidigt 1600-tal saknade staden gästgiveri; borgarna måste husera resande, och Karl IX:s hovfolk togs emot utan ersättning. Protesterna 1609 ledde till privilegiebrev 13 februari 1609 åt förste gästgivaren Jocim Smock från Tyskland; Smockrummet bär fortfarande hans namn. Tomten ligger på mark från kartusianerklostret Pax Mariae (avvecklat ca 1520-tal), som gett Mariefred sitt namn; vid 1980-talsrenoveringen hittades klosterlämningar, delvis bevarade i vinkällaren. Nuvarande huvudbyggnad främst 1700-tal; återinvigning 1989 efter omfattande restaurering. Ett av Sveriges äldsta värdshus i kontinuerlig drift — kungligheter, köpmän, officerare och resande genom krig, epidemier och ägarbyten. Mörk historia som kontext (ej paranormala påståenden): århundraden av vanliga dödsfall, sjukdom och olyckor samt Mariefreds och slottets dramatiska bakgrund.
places.legendSv: FOLKLORE & VITTNESMÅL (ej vetenskapligt verifierat): Fotsteg i tomma korridorer, röster, dörrar som öppnas eller stängs, köldfläckar, känsla av att bli iakttagen, och figurer i munkvanor — ofta knutna till kartusianermunkar från Pax Mariae. Rum 115 och 210 samt vinkällaren nämns oftast; gäster berättar om täcken som rör sig som om de stoppas om. Slottsanekdoter i regionen (t.ex. rörliga dörrvred) behandlas som närliggande folklore, inte som bevis för värdshuset. Atmosfär: träinteriörer, antikt, ljusstakar, tysta korridorer efter midnatt — starkast höst, vinter och regn.
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummarySv: Gripsholms värdshus i Mariefred är ett av Sveriges äldsta värdshus i drift — privilegier 13 februari 1609 under Karl IX, invid Gripsholms slott på mark från klostret Pax Mariae. I över 400 år har resande och kungligheter gästat huset. Folklore och vittnesmål talar om fotsteg, röster, kalla fläckar och munkgestalter — särskilt rum 115, 210 och vinkällaren — medan Haunted Sweden håller isär dokumenterad historia och legend. Boka officiellt; höst- och vinternätter med promenad mot slottet gör platsen idealisk för övernattningsutredning.
places.safetyNoteSv: Aktivt historiskt hotell och restaurang – boka endast via officiella kanaler. Respektera gäster, personal, brandskydd och nattlig tystnad. Filma eller utred inte i korridorer, vinkällare eller andras rum utan tillstånd; önskemål om rum (t.ex. 115 eller 210) beror på tillgång. places.name: Home Hotel Bilan
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Home Hotel Bilan in central Karlstad is one of Sweden's best-known haunted hotels — housed inside Värmland's former county cellular prison (Länscellfängelset), opened in 1847 with about 80 cells and closed as a prison in 1968. The building later served psychiatric care before conversion to a hotel (Hotell Bilan from 1985; today Home Hotel Bilan), preserving thick walls, iron-door atmosphere and a small prison museum in the basement. Documented dark history includes the Silbodal priest Anders Lindbäck: convicted of arsenic poisonings in the 1860s, sentenced to death, and dying by suicide in his cell on 20 November 1865 while awaiting execution. Folklore says his presence never left; hotel and media stories often link unexplained experiences to former cell areas — especially room 204 in contemporary marketing — with staff and guest reports of footsteps, cold spots, cell-door sounds and an oppressive feel in older vaults. Haunted Sweden separates court and prison records from witness accounts and legend. Book officially for one of Sweden's strongest overnight investigation settings.
places.whyItFitsHauntedSweden: Flagship Värmland haunted accommodation: authentic former länsfängelse (1847–1968), preserved cellular architecture, prison museum, psychiatric-ward phase, and Sweden's signature Arsenic Priest legend tied to documented prisoner Anders Lindbäck. Visual rating 9/10, historical value and dark history 10/10, paranormal reputation 9/10, overnight investigation potential 10/10 — Haunted Sweden Score 9.6. Premium content potential EXTREMELY HIGH; research confidence HIGH. Ideal verification mission: overnight, EVP in former corridors and basement, museum visit, staff interviews, compare guest reports with historical records.
places.shortDescription: Karlstad's former county prison (1847) turned hotel — original cells, prison museum, and the Arsenic Priest legend of Anders Lindbäck.
places.history: DOCUMENTED: Home Hotel Bilan occupies Karlbergsgatan 3, Karlstad (Värmland) — the former Länscellfängelset i Karlstad (later Straffängelset i Karlstad), opened 1847 among Sweden's early cellular prisons after the 1844 riksdag reform. Capacity about 81 places (78 light cells, 3 dark/isolation cells); inmate labour historically included bags, matchboxes, brushes and carpentry. From 1911 the larger county cellular prisons including Karlstad were redesignated straffängelse. Kriminalvården left the building in 1968. The property later also served psychiatric care before hotel conversion; Hotell Bilan opened after rebuilding in 1985 (today Home Hotel Bilan / Strawberry). Much original prison character remains: corridor layout, thick stone walls, iron doors, cell volumes adapted as guest rooms, and a small prison museum in the basement. Notable documented inmates include Anders Lindbäck (the Silbodal priest), among others recorded in prison history. ANDERS LINDBÄCK (documented crime & death — not paranormal): Vicar Anders Lindbäck (1803–1865) of Silbodal was convicted in 1865 of murder by arsenic poisoning of parishioners (communion wine and related acts in the mid-1860s; at least three deaths established in court records / biographical sources). Sentenced to death by beheading; while awaiting execution in Karlstad prison he died by suicide by hanging on 20 November 1865. DARK HISTORY (documented context): solitary cellular confinement, illness and despair among inmates, executions sentenced by Swedish courts in the era (Lindbäck's sentence was not carried out due to suicide), and later psychiatric use of the building add layers of isolation and suffering — Haunted Sweden does not invent hauntings from these facts alone.
places.legend: FOLKLORE & WITNESS REPORTS (not scientifically verified): Local and hotel tradition holds that Anders Lindbäck's spirit never left the prison; he remains the building's most famous ghost story (the Arsenic Priest / Silbodal priest). Contemporary hotel and media coverage often associates unexplained experiences with former cell areas — room 204 is highlighted in Strawberry/Home Hotel marketing as linked to Lindbäck folklore. Staff and guest reports over many years describe: reluctance to enter certain basement areas alone; feeling watched in former prison sections; cold spots; footsteps in empty corridors; unexplained sounds from cell doors; strange shadows; and an uncomfortable atmosphere in old prison vaults. Mediums and Halloween promotions have amplified the legend; Haunted Sweden treats these as folklore and anecdotal witness reports, not proven paranormal events. SPECIAL AREAS: former prison cells (guest rooms / detention volumes — most reported experiences); basement vaults (strong historical atmosphere, frequently mentioned by staff); museum area (prison history displays); historic corridors (footsteps and unusual sounds). ATMOSPHERE: original prison corridors, cells as rooms, thick walls, iron doors, preserved architecture, museum authenticity, hush after midnight — one of Sweden's most unique overnight stays. INVESTIGATION IDEAS: overnight in the prison hotel; focus on Lindbäck legend vs records; EVP in former cells and corridors; basement night session; museum after dark (with permission); compare guest reports with court and prison history. BEST CONDITIONS: overnight, autumn evenings, winter darkness, rain, quiet weekdays. Keep DOCUMENTED prison/Lindbäck facts separate from FOLKLORE above.
places.safetyNote: Active hotel — book only through official channels (Home Hotel Bilan / Strawberry). Respect guests, staff, fire rules and night quiet. Do not film or investigate in corridors, basement museum areas or other guests' rooms without permission; room requests (including 204) depend on availability. Basement and museum access follow hotel rules.
places.shortDescriptionSv: Karlstads tidigare länscellfängelse (1847) som hotell — ursprungliga celler, fängelsemuseum och legenden om arsenikprästen Anders Lindbäck.
places.historySv: DOKUMENTERAT: Home Hotel Bilan, Karlbergsgatan 3 i Karlstad — tidigare Länscellfängelset (senare Straffängelset) i Karlstad, öppnat 1847 efter 1844 års fängelsereform. Bevarad fängelsekaraktär, källarmuseum. Mörk historia som kontext: cellisolering, sjukdom, förtvivlan, dödsdomar i tiden och senare psykiatrisk användning — ej automatiska spökpåståenden.
places.legendSv: FOLKLORE & VITTNESMÅL (ej vetenskapligt verifierat): Legenden säger att Anders Lindbäcks ande aldrig lämnade fängelset — hotellets mest kända spökhistoria. Rum 204 lyfts fram i hotellmarknadsföring. Rapporter: personal undviker vissa källarutrymmen ensamma; känsla av att bli iakttagen; köldfläckar; fotsteg; ljud från celldörrar; skuggor; tung atmosfär i valv. Behandlas som vittnesmål och folklore, inte bevis. OMRÅDEN: cellrum, källarvalv, museum, korridorer.
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummarySv: Home Hotel Bilan i Karlstad — Värmlands tidigare länscellfängelse från 1847, hotell sedan 1980-talet med bevarade celler och museum. Dokumenterat dog arsenikprästen Anders Lindbäck i sin cell 1865 medan han väntade på avrättning; folklore säger att han aldrig lämnade huset. Gäst- och personalberättelser om fotsteg, köld och källarvalv gör Bilan till ett av Sveriges mest omtalade spökhotell — historia och legend hålls isär. Boka officiellt för övernattningsutredning.
places.safetyNoteSv: Aktivt hotell – boka endast via officiella kanaler. Respektera gäster, personal, brandskydd och nattlig tystnad. Filma eller utred inte i korridorer, källarmuseum eller andras rum utan tillstånd; önskemål om rum (t.ex. 204) beror på tillgång. Källare och museum enligt hotellets regler.

places.name: Torpa Stenhus
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Torpa Stenhus beside Lake Åsunden near Länghem is one of Sweden's best-preserved medieval stone castles — begun around 1470 by councillor Arvid Knutsson as a fortified stronghold, expanded in the 1500s–1600s, and held by the Stenbock family through inheritance for centuries without commercial sale. In 1552 Gustav Vasa took his third wife, Katarina Stenbock, from Torpa. Visitors come for Renaissance interiors, the Great Hall, baroque chapel and lakeside setting — and for western Sweden's most famous castle ghost lore: the Grey Lady in the upper halls, the Walled-In Girl of plague folklore, and Little Gustav, said to have drowned in a well aged three. Guides tell the stories freely; Haunted Sweden keeps documented building and dynastic history clearly separate from legend and visitor reports of footsteps, cold spots and shadow figures. Book official tours; autumn fog and blue hour after sunset make Torpa a flagship Haunted Sweden destination.
places.whyItFitsHauntedSweden: Western Sweden flagship: outstanding medieval preservation, 500+ years of documented history, Stenbock/Vasa royal connection, multiple named ghost legends with high storytelling power, visitor accessibility via official tours. Visual rating 10/10, historical value and folklore strength 10/10, paranormal reputation 9/10, night investigation potential 9.5/10 — Haunted Sweden Score 9.7. Premium content potential EXTREMELY HIGH; research confidence HIGH. Future verification: full photography, evening investigation with permission, EVP in Great Hall, guide interviews, archive research, drone of castle and Åsunden landscape.
places.shortDescription: One of Sweden's finest medieval stone castles on Lake Åsunden — Stenbock heritage, Gustav Vasa's Katarina, and legendary ghosts including the Grey Lady.
places.history: DOCUMENTED: Torpa Stenhus (Torpa Gård, Länghem, Tranemo municipality, Västra Götaland / Västergötland) stands west of Lake Åsunden. The first stone house was built around 1470 by riksråd Arvid Knutsson as a defensive and trading stronghold amid Danish war threats and local unrest; a parchment letter of 9 February 1513 from Vadstena is among the earliest archival mentions of the stone house at Torpa. Around mid-1500s the stair tower was added; late-1500s works raised roofs, added a fourth storey and decorated halls. Torpa became the principal stamgods of the Stenbock family and has never been sold commercially — inheritance on male or female lines from the medieval builders to the present owners. In 1552, after visiting Torpa, Gustav Vasa chose Katarina Stenbock (daughter of Gustav Olofsson Stenbock and Brita Leijonhufvud) as his third wife — she was collected/taken from Torpa into royal marriage. Early 1600s mark a golden age; Gustav Otto Stenbock later preferred a timber residence for comfort while using the stone house for representation. The castle chapel in Caroline baroque was completed for consecration in 1699 under Christina Katarina de la Gardie after Gustav Otto's death. Surviving fabric includes massive medieval walls, Renaissance Great Hall (riddarsalen), thick oak doors, stair tower and chapel — among Sweden's best-preserved manor castles of the type. DARK HISTORY (documented context, not hauntings): medieval fortification and warfare climate, noble politics, centuries of ordinary illness and death in an isolated lakeside stronghold, and family tragedies recorded in genealogy and local history form the emotional backdrop — Haunted Sweden does not treat folklore deaths as proven events.
places.legend: FOLKLORE (castle tradition / official ghost pages — not documented history): THE GREY LADY (Gråa frun / Grå damen): Said to be a lord's daughter who loved a Danish prisoner her father had brought home; when he killed the captive she died of grief and still wanders the halls as a silent woman in grey, often linked to upper floors after dark — one of Torpa's oldest surviving ghost traditions. THE WALLED-IN GIRL (Den inmurade flickan): Legend of a knight's daughter bricked up alive after returning from Denmark and mentioning plague on her ship; her father feared contagion. Versions vary (sister confided in, night awakening, masons, chair by a window). She is said to wander seeking freedom — clearly folklore, not proven burial. LITTLE GUSTAV (Lille Gustav Stenbock): Local legend that young Gustav, first-born son of Gustaf Otto Stenbock, drowned in a well at age three; visitors (especially women, in site lore) report a pale boy in historic clothing. RELATED FOLKLORE also names white horses before an owner's death and Greve Gustaf Otto Stenbock (portrait / midnight calling tale) — secondary to the three focus legends above. WITNESS REPORTS & GUIDES (unverified): footsteps in empty corridors, doors opening unexpectedly, shadow figures, cold spots, feeling watched — shared by guides, visitors and staff in haunted-castle lists. SPECIAL AREAS: Great Hall; upper floors (Grey Lady); corridors; former well area (Little Gustav); exterior courtyard after sunset. ATMOSPHERE: stone walls, Renaissance hall, ancient stairs, oak doors, Åsunden views, fog on the grounds. INVESTIGATION IDEAS: evening visit with permission; Grey Lady / Walled-In Girl / Little Gustav story mapping vs archives; EVP in Great Hall; castle after dark only when allowed. BEST CONDITIONS: autumn evenings, heavy fog, winter darkness, rain, blue hour. Separate DOCUMENTED history from FOLKLORE above.
places.safetyNote: Privately owned historic castle — visit only via official openings, guided tours and booked events (torpastenhus.se). Stay on permitted paths; do not enter closed floors, climb walls or trespass after hours. Respect staff, other visitors and photography rules. Night investigation only with explicit permission.
places.shortDescriptionSv: Ett av Sveriges finaste medeltida stenhus vid Åsunden — Stenbock-arv, Gustav Vasas Katarina och legendariska spöken som Gråa frun.
places.historySv: DOKUMENTERAT: Torpa Stenhus vid sjön Åsunden, Länghem (Tranemo, Västra Götaland). Första stenhuset ca 1470 av riksrådet Arvid Knutsson som försvars- och handelsborg; omnämnt i pergamentbrev 9 februari 1513. Trapptorn och tillbyggnader 1500–1600-tal; renässansriddarsal; slottskapell invigt 1699. Stenbockarnas stamgods — aldrig sålt, endast ärvt. 1552 hämtade Gustav Vasa sin tredje hustru Katarina Stenbock från Torpa. Mörk historia som kontext: medeltida krigshot, adelspolitik, sjukdom och familjetragedier — inte automatiska spökbevis.
places.legendSv: FOLKLORE (ej dokumenterad historia): GRÅA FRUN — herrdotter som älskade en dansk fånge; vandrar i grått, ofta övre våningar. DEN INMURADE FLICKAN — riddardotter inmurad levande efter pestoro från Danmark; söker frihet — legend. LILLE GUSTAV STENBOCK — drunknade i brunnen som treåring enligt sägen; blek pojke i gamla kläder. VITTNESMÅL: fotsteg, dörrar, skuggor, köld — guider och besökare. Håll isär från dokumenterad byggnads- och ätteshistoria.
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummarySv: Torpa Stenhus vid Åsunden är ett av Sveriges bäst bevarade medeltida stenhus — uppfört ca 1470, Stenbockarnas stamgods, och platsen där Gustav Vasa 1552 hämtade Katarina Stenbock. Hit kommer besökare för renässanssalar och för västra Sveriges mest kända slottsspöken: Gråa frun, den inmurade flickan och lille Gustav. Haunted Sweden skiljer dokumenterad historia från folklore. Boka officiella visningar; höstdimma och blåtimme gör Torpa till en flaggskeppsdestination.
places.safetyNoteSv: Privatägt historiskt slott – besök endast via officiella öppningar, guidade visningar och bokade evenemang. Håll dig till tillåtna stigar; gå inte in på stängda våningar, klättra inte på murar eller trespassera efter stängning. Respektera personal, besökare och fotoregler. Nattutredning endast med uttryckligt tillstånd.

places.name: Ericsbergs Slott
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Ericsbergs Slott near Katrineholm is one of Sweden's finest Baroque castles — first recorded in 1508 as Pintorp (Pinnatorp), rebuilt from the 1650s under Baron Eric Gyllenstierna and completed by his widow Beata von Yxkull, who renamed the estate Ericsberg after her husband. Their son Christoffer Gyllenstierna expanded it in Baroque style; later Hildebrand and then the Bonde family (owners to this day) restored and preserved the house and its celebrated late-17th-century park of avenues, gardens and fountains. Documented history meets Sweden's most famous castle-mistress ghost tradition: Pintorpafrun — folklore variously naming Anna Karlsdotter or Beata von Yxkull as a cruel lady of the manor who returns as a restless female spirit. Historians note the legend is a travelling tale of harsh noblewomen, and that sources do not prove Beata was cruel. Haunted Sweden keeps estate records separate from legend and visitor reports of apparitions, footsteps and cold spots. The castle interior is private; park, café and guided tours open in designated periods — respect restricted grounds.
places.whyItFitsHauntedSweden: Södermanland flagship: outstanding Baroque architecture and park (visual 10/10), 500+ years from Pintorp to Ericsberg, Bonde ownership continuity, and home of the Pintorpafrun — one of Sweden's best-known castle ghost legends (folklore strength 10/10). Historical value 10/10, paranormal reputation 9/10, night investigation potential 9/10 around public park areas — Haunted Sweden Score 9.6. Premium content potential EXTREMELY HIGH; research confidence HIGH. Future mission: park photography, evening public-area investigation, archive research, guide interviews, compare Pintorpafrun variants.
places.shortDescription: Södermanland's great Baroque castle — once Pintorp, still Bonde-owned, and home of Sweden's legendary Pintorpafrun.
places.history: DOCUMENTED: Ericsbergs Slott (Gårdskontoret Ericsberg, 641 93 Katrineholm, Södermanland) stands on the former Pintorp / Pinnatorp estate, mentioned in 1508 when Knut Nilsson of Bosgård sold the croft to Anna Karlsdotter (Vinstorpaätten), widow of knight Erik Eriksson Gyllenstierna; it remained in the Gyllenstierna sphere. The present castle was begun in the mid-1600s by riksråd Baron Eric (Erik Karlsson) Gyllenstierna (d. 1657) and finished by his wife Beata von Yxkull (1618–1667), who renamed the property Ericsberg in his honour while managing the estate during and after his wartime absences. Their son Christoffer (Kristofer) Gyllenstierna, riksråd and överståthållare, remodelled and winged the house in Baroque fashion (architect attributions vary — Nicodemus Tessin the Elder, Jean de la Vallée or Mathias Spihler appear in secondary sources) and developed the French-inspired park, essentially complete after the castle works of the 1680s. After the Gyllenstierna line died out (1733), David Henrik Hildebrand purchased Ericsberg, enlarged the lands and made it a fideikommiss (1778); in 1808 it passed to the Bonde family, who still own the estate (fideikommiss wound up after 1988). 19th-century restorations (e.g. 1812, 1862, 1897 with Isak Gustaf Clason) secured its reputation as one of Sweden's most important Baroque castle environments, including a noted Nordic-history library. The Baroque park — linden avenues, gardens, fountains — dates from the late 1600s. ACCESSIBILITY: the castle itself is privately owned and not generally open; park, café and guided tours operate in designated opening periods — respect private property. DARK HISTORY (documented context): centuries of noble life, inheritance and estate management, deaths of owners across generations, and folklore of harsh treatment of servants and tenants attached to the Pintorp name — Haunted Sweden does not treat legendary cruelty as proven biography.
places.legend: FOLKLORE — PINTORPAFRUN (one of Sweden's most famous castle-ghost traditions; not established fact): A cruel (or, in softer tellings, misunderstood) mistress who mistreated servants and tenant farmers, was punished after death, and wanders as a restless female spirit. The name plays on Pintorp / 'pina' (to torment). Candidates in tradition include Anna Karlsdotter (16th c.), Beata von Yxkull (most often named in popular lore), and even Anna Gustafsdotter Banér (never resident at Pintorp). Scholarly and popular histories stress that the tale is a widespread Swedish wandering legend of harsh noblewomen applied to strong widows who ran estates; there is no documentary proof that Beata von Yxkull was cruel. WITNESS REPORTS & LOCAL STORIES (unverified): female apparition near the castle, unexplained footsteps, cold spots, feeling watched, strange sounds in empty rooms, unusual evening atmosphere — associated with Pintorpafrun in regional ghost lists. SPECIAL AREAS: castle exterior (sighting lore); Baroque park pathways; historic courtyard; linden avenues (isolation and drama after sunset). ATMOSPHERE: magnificent Baroque architecture, historic park and avenues, gardens and fountains, quiet countryside, fog on the grounds, photogenic mystery at blue hour. INVESTIGATION IDEAS: map Pintorpafrun variants vs documented owners; evening photography in public park areas only; EVP outdoors with permission; history-vs-folklore documentary. BEST CONDITIONS: autumn evenings, heavy fog, winter darkness, rain, blue hour. Keep DOCUMENTED estate history separate from FOLKLORE above.
places.safetyNote: Privately owned estate — the castle interior is not generally open to the public. Use only official openings for the Baroque park, café and guided tours (ericsberg.se). Stay on permitted paths; do not enter restricted buildings, courtyards or areas after closing. Respect private property, staff and other visitors. Night investigation only in public/open areas with permission.
places.shortDescriptionSv: Sörmlands stora barockslott — en gång Pintorp, fortfarande Bondeägt, och hem för legenden om Pintorpafrun.
places.historySv: DOKUMENTERAT: Ericsbergs slott vid Katrineholm, tidigare Pintorp/Pinnatorp (omnämnt 1508 när Knut Nilsson sålde torpet till Anna Karlsdotter). Nuvarande slott påbörjat på 1650-talet av friherre Eric Gyllenstierna, färdigställt av hustrun Beata von Yxkull som namngav Ericsberg efter maken. Sonen Christoffer Gyllenstierna byggde om i barock och anlade park. Hildebrand köpte på 1700-talet; från 1808 ätten Bonde, som äger godset än idag. Ett av Sveriges viktigaste barockslott med park från sent 1600-tal. Tillgänglighet: slottet privat; park, café och guidade visningar under öppettider. Mörk historia som kontext: adelsliv, arv och folklore om hård behandling av tjänstefolk — ej bevisad biografi.
places.legendSv: FOLKLORE — PINTORPAFRUN (en av Sveriges mest kända slottsägner, ej fakta): Grym (eller missförstådd) fru som pinade tjänstefolk och torpare och går igen. Namnet knyts till Pintorp. Traditionen pekar på Anna Karlsdotter eller Beata von Yxkull; forskare betonar att det är en vandringssägen och att Beata saknar belägg för grymhet. VITTNESMÅL: kvinnlig gestalt, fotsteg, köld, känsla av att bli iakttagen. OMRÅDEN: slottsfasad, barockpark, gård, lindalléer. Håll isär från dokumenterad godshistoria.
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummarySv: Ericsbergs slott nära Katrineholm är ett av Sveriges finaste barockslott — dokumenterat som Pintorp 1508, ombyggt från 1650-talet under Gyllenstierna och Beata von Yxkull, senare Hildebrand och Bonde. Hit hör legenden om Pintorpafrun, Sveriges mest kända pinande slottsfru — folklore, inte bevisad historia. Park och visningar under öppettider; slottet privat. Haunted Sweden skiljer arkiv från sägen.
places.safetyNoteSv: Privatägt gods – slottsinteriören är i regel stängd. Använd endast officiella öppningar för barockparken, café och guidade visningar. Håll dig till tillåtna stigar; gå inte in i stängda byggnader eller områden efter stängning. Respektera privat egendom. Nattutredning endast i öppna/allmänna områden med tillstånd.

places.name: Dylta Bruk
places.hauntedSwedenAppSummary: Dylta Bruk, about 15 km north of Örebro in Axberg parish (Närke), is Sweden's oldest sulphur works — deposits found in the late 1570s under Duke Charles (later Charles IX), with industrial production starting in 1583. For centuries it was the country's only sulphur mill, also producing alum, vitriol and Dylta red pigment (from 1586, long before Falu rödfärg fame; red-paint production lasted into the 1940s). The landscape still holds mine openings, industrial remains, workers' buildings, a clock tower from the former bruk church, a historic cemetery, and a manor mainly of the 1700s remodelled in the 1850s. Local folklore centres on Kung Jans Källa — a Trinity spring tradition linked to King Johan III and healing water, even though the mill itself began after the legendary 1576 plague visit. Documented labour was harsh: underground mining, sulphur fumes and generations living at the works. Haunted Sweden separates industrial records from spring legends and atmospheric witness reports. Visit as cultural heritage — respect private manor areas and mine safety.
places.whyItFitsHauntedSweden: A different Haunted Sweden destination beyond castles and churches: nationally significant industrial heritage (riksintresse), 400+ years of documented sulphur and pigment industry, preserved manor–mine–cemetery landscape, and Kung Jans Källa folklore. Visual 8.5/10, historical value and industrial heritage 10/10, folklore 8/10, paranormal reputation 7.5/10 — Haunted Sweden Score 8.8. Premium content potential HIGH; research confidence HIGH. Future mission: exterior and mine-entrance documentation, EVP near industrial buildings (safely), spring visit, local historians, drone of the estate.
places.shortDescription: Sweden's first sulphur works (1583) north of Örebro — mines, manor, cemetery and the healing-spring lore of Kung Jans Källa.
places.history: DOCUMENTED: Dylta Bruk (718 97 Dyltabruk, Axbergs socken, Örebro municipality, Närke) began after sulphur ore (svavelkis) was found southeast of Dylta village in the late 1570s within Duke Charles's duchy. The duke ordered a sulphur works; construction 1580–1582, production from 1583 — long Sweden's only sulphur mill and a key source for gunpowder sulphur, later export surplus. Vitriol, alum (Bastian Heisler from Germany, 1586) and red-paint burning (from 1586; continued until c. 1941–1942) made Dylta one of Sweden's earliest chemical industries. Crown, then leaseholders from Hans Leffler (1631); Henrik Barckhusen received privileges from Queen Christina (1649), including the right of the royal family to lodge at Dylta during epidemics because sulphur smoke was believed to keep contagion away — a documented privilege distinct from the Johan III spring legend. Later Casten Feif, then the Åkerhielm family for ~275 years from 1739; from 2014 related Roos ownership. The estate formed its own bruk parish/chapel congregation for periods (own preacher from early eras; parish roughly 1688–1818); church later demolished — clock tower (klockstapel, 1714) and cemetery (from 1712, still in use) remain. Manor (corps de logi) mainly 1700s, remodelled mid-1800s; 'Klostret' likely a 1500s storehouse, now museum. Mining and industrial traces survive as an industrimuseum within a riksintresse cultural environment; modern estate focuses on forestry, aquaculture, hunting and property. DARK HISTORY (documented context): centuries of dangerous underground mining, sulphur fumes, hard labour, industrial accidents, and workers who lived their lives at the isolated mill community — plus the historic cemetery of the bruk congregation — without inventing hauntings from these facts.
places.legend: FOLKLORE — KUNG JANS KÄLLA (not verified as royal or medicinal fact): Local tradition says King Johan III (and sometimes Katarina Jagellonica) fled plague to Dylta around 1576 and visited a spring later called Kung Jans Källa. The spring became a Trefaldighetskälla — people gathered on Trinity Eve believing the water had healing powers. Site heritage texts note the tale's timing problem: the sulphur works did not exist until the early 1580s, so the 1576 'escape to the mill' story is legend, even if plague-refuge privileges appear later in 1649 documents for different reasons (sulphur smoke). WITNESS REPORTS & ATMOSPHERE (unverified): feeling watched near abandoned industrial buildings; unusual silence around old mines; strange sounds at the former sulphur works; heavy atmosphere in preserved buildings; local lore of former workers; cemetery and industrial landscape stories. SPECIAL AREAS: former sulphur works; old mine area (dangerous — do not enter workings); historic manor (private residence); cemetery; Kung Jans Källa. ATMOSPHERE: manor, mine mouths, industrial buildings, forest, quiet countryside, clock tower, fog on mill grounds. INVESTIGATION IDEAS: map industrial timeline vs spring folklore; safe exterior night walk; EVP near buildings not inside mines; photograph cemetery and tower with respect. BEST CONDITIONS: autumn evenings, heavy fog, rain, winter darkness, early morning mist. Keep DOCUMENTED industry separate from FOLKLORE above.
places.safetyNote: Active private estate and cultural heritage site — follow official visitor information (dyltabruk.se). Do not enter mine openings, shafts or unstable industrial structures. Respect the private manor, cemetery etiquette and closed buildings. Stay on permitted paths; no trespassing after hours. Night investigation only in publicly accessible outdoor areas with permission.
places.shortDescriptionSv: Sveriges första svavelbruk (1583) norr om Örebro — gruvor, herrgård, kyrkogård och sägnen om Kung Jans källa.
places.historySv: DOKUMENTERAT: Dylta bruk, Axbergs socken, Örebro kommun (Närke). Svavelkis hittades sent 1570-tal i hertig Karls hertigdöme; svavelbruk 1580–1582, drift från 1583 — länge landets enda. Även vitriol, alun och rödfärg (från 1586 till ca 1941–42). Privilegier 1649 (bl.a. kungligt logi vid farsoter p.g.a. svavelrök). Åkerhielm i ~275 år; idag släktägande. Bruksförsamling periodvis; klockstapel 1714 och kyrkogård från 1712 kvar. Herrgård 1700-tal, ombyggd 1850-tal. Riksintresse industrimiljö med museum. Mörk historia som kontext: farlig gruvdrift, svavelrök, slitsamt arbete och isolerat brukssamhälle — ej automatiska spökpåståenden.
places.legendSv: FOLKLORE — KUNG JANS KÄLLA: Sägen om Johan III:s pestflykt till Dylta ca 1576 och en helgekälla (trefaldighetskälla). Kulturmiljötexter påpekar att svavelbruket inte fanns då — legenden är alltså tidsmässigt problematisk jämfört med dokumenterad drift från 1583.
